title: Streptococcus Viridans meningitis in an immunocompetent child: A case report
case_prompt:
A previously healthy 5-year-old boy presented with a 2-day history of headaches, recurrent vomiting, fever to 38.5 °C, weakness, loss of appetite, and photophobia. He was born at 30 weeks’ gestation (birth weight 1200 g) and had normal developmental milestones; he underwent strabismus repair at age 3. There was no recent history of diarrhea, constipation, otolaryngeal symptoms, or head trauma.

On examination, he was alert but appeared weak. Temperature 38.5 °C, heart rate 120 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, SpO₂ 95% on room air. Moderate nuchal rigidity and a positive Brudzinski sign were present; cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. Funduscopic examination showed no papilledema.

Laboratory studies revealed neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis, normal ESR and CRP, and normal serum electrolytes. Noncontrast head CT and subsequent brain MRI were unremarkable. Empiric therapy with ceftriaxone, vancomycin, acyclovir, and dexamethasone was initiated. A lumbar puncture yielded clear cerebrospinal fluid with 130 white blood cells per high-power field (96% neutrophils), glucose 49 mg/dL, and protein 121 mg/dL.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of common pediatric meningitis pathogens — “In older children and adults, the prevalence of S. pneumonia, Neisseria meningitis, and Hemophilus influenza increases.”  
2. Concern for culture contamination — “The presence of a single positive streptococcal meningitis culture from CSF or blood is considered contamination; however, in our case, we had clear symptoms as well as a positive extraction and successful treatment that pointed to the presence of S. viridans.”  
3. Evaluation of otolaryngeal infection as a source — “One study found that half of the patients with S. viridans meningitis had a previous otolaryngeal infection as a possible transmission route, but this was not the case in our patient.”  
4. Assessment of surgical or traumatic entry — “A trauma or surgical procedure could result in an S. viridans infection in an adult.”  
5. Interpretation of CSF glucose level — “In our patient, the glucose level was nearly normal, which is indicative of the fact that glucose levels in S. viridans meningitis can vary.”  
6. Use of ESR in early presentation — “We must consider that a normal ESR could not possibly rule out an active infection.”  
7. Exclusion of subdural empyema — “In patients with bacterial meningitis, cerebral subdural empyema (SDE) is uncommon, although infections caused by S. viridans are more likely to induce the condition (which did not develop in this patient).”  
8. Ruling out endocarditis — “They are a common cause of infective endocarditis and critical infections in immunocompromised populations.” (No abnormalities on echocardiography.)
